blocks.text: When we read that Bagoas found the trunk of Holofernes thrown down ἐπὶ τῆς χετλωνίδος [epi tēs chetlōnidos], Iudith. XIV, 13., others rightly observe that in place of χετλωνίδος [chetlōnidos], a meaningless word, we should read χελωνίδος [chelōnidos], as Hesychius and Suidas read it, and that χελωνίς [chelōnis] is so called ἀπὸ τῆς χελώνης [apo tēs chelōnēs], from the tortoise. But what exactly a χελωνὶς [chelōnis] is, is not sufficiently clear. The Vulgate translator renders it cortina [curtain]. Most of the more recent interpreters render it stratum [couch] or lectus [bed]; they are easily refuted. For Judith had cut off Holofernes' head, καὶ ἐπεκύλισε τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς στρωμνῆς [kai epekylise to sōma autou apo tēs strōmnēs], and had rolled his body off the couch, ch. 13, v. 10. Therefore the χελωνὶς [chelōnis], in which Bagoas found this body ἐῤῥιμμένον [erhrimmenon], thrown down, is something different from the couch and the bed. Hesychius, under χελωνίδος [chelōnidos], explains it as οὐδὸς τῆς θύρας τῆς σκηνῆς [oudos tēs thyras tēs skēnēs], the threshold of the door of the tent. So Suidas too must be corrected from him, since he writes ὅδου [hodou] for οὐδοῦ [oudou]. This is hardly likely, both because the name does not fit, and because Holofernes' body was rolled from the couch into the chelonis. The chelonis, then, was not near the threshold of the door, but in the innermost part of the tent, where the commander's bed itself also stood. Not to detain the reader any longer: to me the χελωνὶς [chelōnis] is קבה kubba. The word occurs once in Scripture and is not well understood, namely Num. XXV, 8., where, while Zimri and Kozbi were fornicating, Phinehas went אל הקבה, into the kubba, and pierced them both through. Different people explain this differently. But among the Arabs قبة [qubba] kubba, or kobba, and with the article القبة [al-qubba] alkobba, is a chamber of vaulted work, by which a bed is enclosed. The Spaniards call it alcoba [II, 523] and alcova, a word which among us too has a similar meaning. The root قب [qabba] kabba in the second conjugation means to vault, or to build vaulted work. So, just as the musical instrument χέλυς [chelys], or testudo [tortoise], is called in Arabic العود [al-ʿūd] alaud, whence the Spanish laud or laut, and our lut, so القبة [al-qubba] alkobba, [col. 1093] or the chamber we have described, is called in Arabic by another name ام العود [umm al-ʿūd] ommolaudi, that is, mother of the tortoise, because it is of vaulted, tortoise-shaped work. Among the Arabs the bridal chamber is in such an القبة [al-qubba] alkobba. And leading the bride there is called بنا [banā] bana and زف [zaff] zappha. So Holofernes' bedchamber, when he was about to lie with Judith, as he thought, was in an alcobba of this kind; and why it is called χελωνὶς [chelōnis] in Greek is now clear to anyone. Perhaps the χελωνὶς [chelōnis] was also named from its material. For in former times tortoise shell was much used in the beds and bedsteads of the great. This luxury, first adopted in the East, finally reached the Romans. The date is noted by Pliny, book 9, chapter 11: To cut tortoise shells into plates, he says, and to veneer beds and sideboards with them, was introduced by Carbilius Pollio. And book 16, [col. 1094] chapter 43: Tortoise shell is cut for this purpose. And recently, in the principate of Nero, it was devised by monstrous ingenuity that it should destroy itself with paints and sell for more by imitating wood. Thus high prices are sought for beds. Hence Martial, book 12, Epigram 67:
Beds jewelled with the finest tortoise shell gleam.
What kind of tortoise swam in the waves of Ocean, to make a splendid and noble headrest for the Trojan-born.

Where the Scholiast says: That he might have a tortoise-shell bed. For the ancients adorned beds with the tortoise shell of Ocean. Apuleius too, not far from the end of book 10: A bed shining with Indian tortoise shell, swelling with a heap of feathers, etc. But this is more than enough on a matter of no great importance. So here we end, and now pass on to the birds.
